decision.detail: I walk past the dark booth—curtain drawn, no light under the door, Alma's space now empty—and into the station room. The patch board is lit, the Pittsburgh line humming green. Rita's already at the adjacent track, her own reel threaded, eyes on the monitor. I don't look at her. I set my reel on the take-up arm, thread the tail through the guide, give the spool one firm push so it seats. The metal is warm from my coat pocket. I don't press play. I don't need to. I heard her voice when the button went down. Thirty seconds of a woman in a booth saying what she needed to say before the lights went out for good. That's the whole tape. I step back. My hands are empty. I unclip my coat, hang it on the hook by the door, and walk out past the ballroom. The lights in there are going, slow and gold, the kind that make you want to stand in the doorway. I don't stop. I get to the street. I walk north. The Rialto sign buzzes off behind me. I don't look back.
decision.intention: Get Alma's voice onto the wire before the line closes. One reel, one take, one city it lands in. After that the camera's dark, the coat's off, the day is over. I'm not the one who has to sit in the ballroom and watch the lights burn down.
